newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU quest swings attention from real problems.
newsitem.headline: EMU quest swings attention from real problems.

text.p: Joblessness is emerging increasingly as the Achilles's heel for those European Union leaders driving their countries relentlessly towards monetary union in 1999.

Analysts say that, rightly or wrongly, tough budgetary discipline and the preconditions for EMU have become closely linked in the mind of the European public with record unemployment levels, even in a country like Germany which had so far been seen as the economic motor of Europe.
"The single currency forces us into a very serious stock-taking," said one German political analyst.
"There is vast dissatisfaction among the public and of course sooner or later the question will be asked what have the politicians done to us." BUDGET REFORM REQUIRED WITH OR WITHOUT EMU
The analysts said that those tough economic decisions being taken by European leaders are needed irrespective of EMU.

"The reality is there is a need for budget consolidation in Europe in order to be prepared for the strains in the next century coming from demographic factors," says Niels Thygesen, economist at Copenhagen University.

Analysts said that record unemployment has come at a time when countries were also battling with problems of an ageing population reared in an increasingly costly welfare state and intense competition from trade rivals across the Atlantic and in the so-called Tiger economies of Asia.

Recent studies from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) show that in 1990 the ratio of older people to those in the work force was 19 percent among industrialised countries. In other words, four workers paid the costs of every pensioner.
By 2030 this ratio is expected to soar to 37 percent, with Germany up to 49.2 percent and Italy at 48.3 percent. LABOUR REFORM NEEDED TOO
Another area of much needed reform is in Europe's inflexible labour markets.

Whether EMU will help to create jobs is debatable. But in a vivid example of how serious the problem is, Britain's Prime Minister John Major recently noted that over the past 20 years the European Union had created only five million new jobs, of which one million were in the private sector.
By contrast, the American economy over the same period produced 36 million new jobs, with 31 million in the private sector.

Many analysts agree the Anglo-American approach towards job creation is not appropriate for continental Europe. But at least a few steps in this direction are needed if monetary union is to stay on course.

"If there are no changes in the institutional arrangements that prevent the labour market from equilibrating supply and demand, future historians will conclude that rising unemployment turned both German and European Monetary Union into economic failures," said a recent study from Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt.

Some observers worry about growing public resentment directed against big business, especially at a time when many firms are relocating their operations abroad to take advantage of relatively cheap labour.
Here again, there has been little direction from the political class on how to turn around this trend and stem its debilitating effect on the average wage earner.

This has been largely demonstrated in the uncertainties about the political future of Germany's veteran Chancellor Helmut Kohl who faces crucial general elections next year in the shadow of a post-war record 12 million German jobless.
It was also seen as a major factor in recent poll victories by extreme right-wing nationalists in southern France.

"If there is no democratic alternative and none of the great parties bring out the real questions, then you have a problem," another German analyst said of the politicians' apparent inability to confront those dire problems.
